reason: The sources provide enough confirmed data to construct a surprising 45-second script with more than 10 dual-sourced claims.
story: Deep in the southern constellation of Phoenix lies a colossal galaxy cluster breaking all the rules of astrophysics. Discovered in 2010 using the South Pole Telescope in Antarctica, the Phoenix Cluster sits billions of light-years away from Earth. Normally, a supermassive black hole at the center of a cluster acts like a cosmic heater, blasting radiation that stops gas from cooling and forming stars. But the Phoenix Cluster defies this rule entirely. Its central galaxy hosts a supermassive black hole weighing roughly 10 billion solar masses, yet it pumps out hundreds of new stars every single year in a frantic starburst. For over a decade, astronomers were baffled because they could only detect ultra-hot gas and ultra-cold gas, with a massive missing link in between. Now, using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, scientists have finally mapped a hidden halo of intermediate warm gas glowing like a neon sign, solving the mystery of this stellar factory.
angle: A colossal galaxy cluster defies the laws of astrophysics by forming hundreds of stars a year while its 10-billion-solar-mass black hole fails to stop it.

claims.claim: The Phoenix Cluster was discovered in 2010.
The cluster was discovered using the South Pole Telescope in Antarctica.
The Phoenix Cluster is located approximately 5.8 billion light-years from Earth.
The cluster has a supermassive black hole at its core weighing roughly 10 billion solar masses.
In typical galaxy clusters, the central black hole prevents gas from cooling enough to form stars.
The central galaxy of the Phoenix Cluster forms hundreds of stars per year at an extreme rate.
Previous observations only detected gas at extreme hot and cold temperature ends.
Researchers used NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to map the missing cooling gas.
JWST used its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and Medium-Resolution Spectrometer.
The missing warm gas glows via neon VI signatures in the mid-infrared spectrum.
The intermediate cooling gas is found at temperatures around 540,000 degrees Fahrenheit (300,000 Celsius).
Confirmation from Webb builds on over a decade of studies using the Chandra X-ray Observatory and Hubble Space Telescope.

disputed: Source 1 lists the comoving distance as 8.61 billion light-years, while Sources 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 state it is 5.8 billion light-years away. The script should use 5.8 billion light-years as it is overwhelmingly supported across multiple recent NASA and astronomical sources.
